messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Enclosed Spaces: Enclosed or confined spaces, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Vignette:
David was a 53-year-old social worker who had spent two decades at a community mental health center, dedicated to helping clients navigate their own darkest moments. The assault happened in a windowless storage room adjacent to his office, a small space he had used to store intake files. A client he had been trying to stabilize for months cornered him there after a session. David still could not find the words to describe what happened, even to himself. The memory came back not as a coherent narrative he could tell his wife or his supervisor, but as a sudden, suffocating wave of raw terror and a crushing sense of shame that left him breathless. In the weeks that followed, he tried to push the whole thing out of his mind, telling himself to just get back to work, that it was part of the job, that he should be able to handle it.

But work became a minefield. The storage room was sealed shut and never used again, but every closed door at the agency now made his chest tighten. He started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, arriving at third-floor meetings drenched in sweat and lightheaded. He began turning down home visits to unfamiliar neighborhoods, offering thin excuses to his supervisor about scheduling conflicts that he could not quite justify to her or to himself. The hypervigilance was exhausting and inescapable. He found himself constantly looking over his shoulder, scanning parking lots as he walked to his car, and reading threat into the smallest delays. If a colleague was five minutes late for a supervision meeting, his mind would instantly race to the worst possible conclusion—that something terrible had happened, that he was in danger again. He had come to believe that the world was neatly divided into safe, known spaces and dangerous, unknown ones, and the territory of the safe ones was steadily shrinking.

At home, a different kind of torture consumed him. He spent hours replaying the assault, not to process what had happened, but to mentally plot a revenge he knew he would never actually take. He would imagine confronting his assailant in vivid detail, and these fantasies left him feeling agitated and morally sickened, yet he could not stop the loop from running. His wife noticed the distance growing between them. He was irritable and withdrawn, staring at the wall during dinner, unable to explain the storm inside him. When she asked what was wrong, he would say “nothing” and force the thoughts down again, a strategy that only deepened his shame and isolation, because he knew the "nothing" was a lie.

By the time David walked into the clinic, what finally brought him in was a quiet ultimatum from his wife, coupled with a formal complaint from his agency director about his declining availability for field visits. He was terrified of being seen as broken or weak—a man who could not protect himself, a social worker who could no longer do the job he had spent his life building. But he was also terrified of staying the same. More than anything, David hoped to find a way to live without the constant vigilance that made his own office feel like a trap, without the shame that made him want to disappear every time a memory surfaced, and without the anger that was slowly poisoning everything he had worked for. He hoped, somehow, to finally find the words.
